Severe Flooding Disrupts Engineering & Construction Sites Across Azerbaijan

Ongoing severe flooding in Azerbaijan has caused significant disruption to the Engineering & Construction industry, with multiple reports of damage to active worksites, equipment yards, and staff accommodations. The event, triggered by days of torrential rainfall and swollen riverbanks, has left several firms struggling to maintain operations as water levels remain dangerously high.

As of Thursday, industry sources confirmed that at least seven major construction projects in the Kur-Araz lowlands and the outskirts of Ganja have been inundated, halting work and damaging on-site machinery. The headquarters of AzBuild Group reported that their primary fabrication plant near Mingachevir is “partially submerged,” with extensive water ingress in storage facilities, leading to concerns over the integrity of both raw materials and finished components.

Workers have also been affected, with temporary housing units at several sites rendered inaccessible or unsafe. According to a spokesperson for the Azerbaijan Construction Workers’ Union, approximately 420 site workers have been evacuated from flooded areas since Tuesday. “Our immediate priority is the safety of our members, but many have already lost personal belongings and, in some cases, vital documentation in the rising waters,” said the spokesperson.

The Azerbaijan Engineering & Construction Association (AECA) issued a statement noting that preliminary assessments indicate “significant structural damage” at multiple active sites, although full evaluations are ongoing. “We are seeing the most severe impacts in low-lying project areas, where floodwaters have compromised foundations, eroded embankments, and left heavy equipment unusable,” said AECA President Elchin Ismayilov. “It is too early to estimate the full extent of the losses, as the flooding continues, but we expect disruptions to persist for several days.”

Industry analysts warn that the ongoing nature of the event could further delay critical project timelines and add to costs. “With water levels still rising in some locations, it will be difficult for firms to resume work or even assess the full scope of the damage,” said Narmin Suleymanova, a sector consultant based in Baku.

Firms are now mobilizing emergency response teams and adapting contingency plans as they await a break in the weather. The AECA has called for urgent government support to help stabilize affected projects and protect industry workers as the flooding continues.
